# Motivation

Biological systems are inherently relational, governed by complex interaction
networks among genes, transcripts, proteins and organisms. The systematic
organisation of this relational metadata within public repositories—such as
UniProt (proteins), Rhea (reactions), and KEGG (metabolic pathways)—provides a
foundational framework for modern computational biology. However, leveraging
these resources in routine bioinformatics workflows is frequently hindered by
fragmented data structures, heterogeneous file formats and data volumes that
exceed local computational capacities. Without a structured approach, navigating
the labyrinth of biological knowledge can feel overwhelming, time-consuming and
discouraging.

`ariadne` addresses these challenges by assembling a reproducible graph of
interlinked biological resources coupled with a robust programmatic toolkit,
which facilitates knowledge-driven annotation, feature stratification and
goal-oriented resource traversal. For example, it enables functional annotation
of microbial features via ChocoPhlAn and the Web of Life (WoL), alongside
feature aggregation using metabolic modules and microbial signatures. By
naturally extending to multi-omics modalities (e.g., metabolites, proteins and
genes), `ariadne` provides a unified interface for integrating prior biological
knowledge into standard Bioconductor workflows (example use cases are presented
in [this vignette](https://minotau-r.github.io/ariadne/articles/use_cases.html)).

# Tutorial

This tutorial demonstrates the programmatic usage of ariadne within R/RStudio.
For extensions in other environments, refer to [ariadnePy](https://github.com/Minotau-R/ariadnePy) for Python and
[ariadneApp](https://github.com/Minotau-R/ariadneApp) for the Shiny web
application.

## Installation

The official Bioconductor release version can be installed as follows:

```{r install-release, eval = FALSE}
if( !requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE) ){
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("ariadne")
```

For the latest functionality, the devel version can be installed as follows:

```{r install-beta, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# Initialise devel version
BiocManager::install(version = "devel")

BiocManager::install("ariadne")
```

## Import and explore the resource graph

`ariadne` combines various databases into a unified graph structure providing
links between biological entities. The mechanism of retrieving and combining
relational data is detailed in
[this vignette](https://minotau-r.github.io/ariadne/articles/resources.html).
In a nutshell, the companion data package `ariadneDB` defines feature types and
houses cross-database mappings formatted as graph objects that are reproducibly
hosted on Zenodo.

```{r lib, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ariadne)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(DT)
```

The resource graph is imported using the `ariadne()` constructor, which returns
the integrated database network as an igraph object.

```{r fetch}
# Import resource graph
graph <- ariadne()
```

The graph topology can also be visualised using `plotPath()`.

```{r plot}
# Plot resource graph
plotPath(graph)
```

Suppose we need to trace relational paths between gene functions and enzymatic activities represented by KEGG Orthologroups (KOs) and Enzyme Commission (EC)
numbers, respectively. The `searchPath()` function identifies the $k$ shortest
paths connecting these entities.

```{r search}
# Search for paths from ko to ec
searchPath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 3)
```

The top three paths include direct KO-EC mappings from KEGG as well as indirect
routes through UniRef50 and UniRef90 from ChocoPhlAn and UniProt. Specific paths
can be filtered and visualised using the `include`, `exclude` and `res.name`
arguments.

```{r plot-path}
plotPath(graph, ko ~ ec, include = "uniref90", prune = TRUE)
```

Because the output is a standard `igraph` object, native graph operations are
fully supported. For instance, we can evaluate node centrality by sorting nodes
according to their degree (total adjacent edges):

```{r degree}
# Find and sort node degrees
node_degrees <- graph |>
    degree(mode = "all") |>
    sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# Select nodes above degree threshold
node_degrees <- node_degrees[node_degrees >= 10]

# View node degrees
kable(node_degrees, col.names = "degree")
```

We can also compute local neighborhood sizes for specific feature types:

```{r neighbour}
# List neighbours of ko node
neighbors(graph, "ko", mode = "all")
```

## Select and customise the resource graph

By default, `ariadne` uses the latest available resource releases.

```{r res-defaults}
# List available resource versions
versions <- listResourceVersions(default = TRUE)

# View versions
datatable(versions)
```

However, historical or specific database releases can be pinned by passing a
named list to the `versions` argument.

```{r res-versions}
# List custom versions
versions <- list(BugSigDB = "v1.2.2", WoL = "v20April2021")

# Import graph with custom versions
graph <- ariadne(versions = versions)
```

Custom resources (including local files) can be integrated into the `ariadne`
graph via `addResource()`. For example, we can incorporate
taxid-to-antimicrobial resistance mappings from the EMBL AMR Portal:

```{r}
# Set URL to custom resource
url <- "https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/amr_portal/releases/2025-12/"
url <- paste0(url, "genotype.csv.gz")

# Add resource to ariadne graph
graph <- addResource(
    graph,
    url,
    res.name = "AMR",
    select = c("taxon_id", "antibiotic_ontology"),
    col.names = c("taxid", "aro")
)

# Search for newly added path
searchPath(graph, taxid ~ aro)
```

## Cross the graph to link biological entities

We decide to go through the simplest path, which corresponds to a `k` of 1. The
links between KO and EC are found by the function `weavePath`, which fetches
the necessary resources and weaves a path from ko to ec.

Selecting the most direct path ($k = 1$), we traverse the graph from KO to EC
using `weavePath()`, which dynamically fetches required backend resources and
constructs the mapping table.

```{r}
# Weave path from ko to ec
ko2ec <- weavePath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 1)
```

The output is returned as a `linkmap`—a tidy, two-column data frame pairing
source and target identifiers, optionally including feature name annotations in
a third column.

```{r}
# View some links
datatable(ko2ec)
```

The weave can be initialised with a set of identifiers belonging to the `from`
id type. This is specified with the argument `init`.

```{r}
# Define custom ko initial values
ko.ids <- c("K00665", "K05913", "K11533")

# Weave path with initial values
ko2ec <- weavePath(graph, ko ~ ec, init = ko.ids)

# View links
knitr::kable(ko2ec)
```

Sometimes, we would like to know how much each origin id covers each target id
in terms of percent coverage (useful for pathway enrichment analysis). This can
be achieved with the alternative function `weaveComplex`. For example, we can
estimate the percentage of kegg pathways covered by different ec ids, and select
only those links above a certain `threshold`.

When evaluating pathway enrichment or metabolic coverage, quantifying
source-to-target representation is essential. The `weaveComplex()` function
estimates feature coverage percentages and allows filtering based on
user-defined thresholds.

```{r}
# Find complex links between ko and kegg pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    ec ~ kegg_path,
    threshold = 0.5
)

# View some links
knitr::kable(ec2path)
```

The resulting mapping can be visualised with the `plotModules()` function.

```{r}
# Visualise links
plotModules(ko2path, layout = "sugiyama") + coord_flip()
```

## Ensure reproducibility of the ariadne workflow

A path table is a metadata object that sufficiently describes the parameters to
reconstruct the complete `ariadne`workflow. The data object `pathMeta` provides
an example of this schema.

```{r pathMeta}
# Import pathMeta object
data("pathMeta", package = "ariadne")

# View pathMeta object
datatable(pathMeta)
```

The `drawPath()` function generates a corresponding path table for any valid
traversal query.

```{r draw}
# Draw path table from ko to ec
path_df <- drawPath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 1)

datatable(path_df)
```
The resulting path table can be directly supplied to `weavePath()` to reproduce
the workflow.

```{r weave-drawn}
ko2ec.simple <- weavePath(path_df)

datatable(ko2ec.simple)
```

Similarly, path tables are compatible with `weaveComplex()` for coverage-based
analyses.

```{r complex-drawn}
ko2ec.complex <- weaveComplex(path_df)

datatable(ko2ec.complex)
```

## Add results to SummarizedExperiment for downstream analyses

ariadne natively integrates with the broader Bioconductor ecosystem, supporting
`SummarizedExperiment` (SE)-derived containers, the `mia` ecosystem for
microbiome data science and the `anansi` package for knowledge-driven
association analysis. We begin by loading the `Tengeler2020` dataset.

```{r}
# Import experiment object
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")

# Rename experiment object
tse <- Tengeler2020

# View experiment object
tse
```

We also import the built-in `butyrate` linkmap, representing a typical output
generated by `ariadne` weave functions.

```{r}
# Import butyrate linkmap
data("butyrate", package = "ariadne")

# View butyrate linkmap
datatable(butyrate)
```

The `getModules()` function maps features to the specified annotation `keys`
(such as Genus or Family), returning a module membership matrix indicating
presence/absence or coverage fractions.

```{r}
# Get butyrate-producer module membership
modules <- getModules(tse, butyrate, key = c("Genus", "Family"))

# View modules table
datatable(modules)
```

Using `addModules()`, this module membership table is incorporated directly into
the experiment side information that can be accessed in downstream analyses.

```{r}
# Add modules to experiment as names instead of ids
tse <- addModules(tse, butyrate, key = "Genus", as = "names")
```

The `mia` package provides specialised methods for set-aware operations. The
`agglomerateByModule()` function aggregates assay abundance tables across
features belonging to specific sets.

```{r}
# Agglomerate features by membership to butyrate-producer set
mod.se <- agglomerateByModule(tse, by = "rows", group = "butyrate")

# Plot abundance of butyrate producers
plotAbundance(mod.se)
```

Additionally, `applyByModule()` enables arbitrary set-wise computations on an
SE object. For example, it is possible to estimate alpha diversity for each
module (only one in this case), which is sometimes called _functional diversity_.

```{r}
# Estimate alpha diversity for each module
tse <- applyByModule(
    tse,
    .by = "rows",
    .group = "butyrate",
    FUN = getAlpha,
    index = c("shannon", "faith"),
    min.group.size = 2
)

# viz functional alpha/beta
plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "shannon_1")
```
